profiles.name: Andrew Lawrence
profiles.description: Andrew Lawrence was a 28-year-old former Peace Corps volunteer and peace activist living at Jonah House in Baltimore, also described as associated with the Community for Creative Non-Violence. On Easter Sunday, April 3, 1988, he joined Philip Berrigan, Sister Margaret McKenna and Gregory Boertje in boarding the USS Iowa with a public tour at Norfolk Naval Station. Calling themselves the Nuclear Navy Plowshares, the four separated from the tour, used hammers and bolt cutters against two armored Tomahawk cruise-missile launcher boxes, poured blood on the equipment and displayed banners reading “Seek the Disarmed Christ” and “Tomahawks Into Plowshares,” stopping when naval security ordered them to. Lawrence was arrested and charged with federal criminal trespass. Although offered release on personal recognizance, he refused and remained jailed in solidarity with Boertje, whose bond had been set at $25,000 over an earlier Plowshares prosecution. Tried without a jury before U.S. Magistrate Tommy Miller, Lawrence admitted the action but argued it was justified by international law and the threat posed by nuclear weapons; he was convicted on May 19, 1988 and sentenced on July 21, 1988 to four months in prison, having by then already spent 109 days in custody. He was then transferred to a Philadelphia jail to face a separate charge connected with hanging a banner from the federal courthouse roof during one of the Epiphany Plowshares trials; his final release date has not been recovered.
profiles.finding: Revolutionary Worker466 reports Nuclear Navy sentencing. Commons actor, Navy ensign and contemporary sports writer photographs not matched to 28-year-old 1988 activist.

profiles.name: Arnold Heightland
profiles.description:
Heightland was a union coal miner involved in a bitter labor dispute in eastern Kentucky that escalated beyond picket-line conflict. Federal prosecutors tied him and other striking miners to an armed ambush of coal trucks during the strike, an attack in which rifle fire struck the vehicles and a truck driver was killed.

He was convicted in federal court under a statute aimed at protecting vehicles used in interstate commerce, based on the conclusion that the ambush intentionally damaged the trucks and was carried out with reckless disregard for human safety. The case became emblematic of how labor conflict in the region intersected with aggressive criminal prosecution when violence erupted around strikebreaking operations.

profiles.name: Donnie Thornsbury
profiles.description:
Donnie Thornsbury is a union miner who was involved in the bitter 15-month strike of the A.T. Massey Coal Company and its subsidiaries in 1984-85. He served as Local 2496 President of United Mine Workers of America (UMWA).

Thornsbury and four other miners were framed for the May 1985 shooting death of scab coal hauler Hayes West. The five were among the most militant miners at the Samoyed Energy Company Mine in Pike County, Kentucky, near the West Virginia border. A number of witnesses testified that the murder was staged by the company to obtain a court injunction against picketing in order to break the strike.

The paid informants alleged that the shots that killed West were fired from the top of a nearby mountain. But West was killed by a blast from a shotgun, a close range weapon, and fatally wounded by ammunition that was generally available only to police and security companies. Witnesses reported seeing guards on the mountain at the time. None testified to seeing any union miners there. There were no fingerprints of the defendants on any of the guns or shell casings allegedly used in the shooting, and the shotgun that was allegedly the murder weapon was never found. While one miner was acquitted, Judge Wilhoit dolled out the maximum sentences for the remaining four despite lack of evidence.
profiles.finding: Same miners group photograph in Militant5201 and Workers Vanguard444 identifies Thornsbury at left. Rights/creator and crop quality pending; unrelated family-history lists not used.

profiles.name: James Darryl Smith
profiles.description:
Smith was prosecuted alongside other striking miners in connection with the same eastern Kentucky coal-truck ambush during a labor conflict. The case focused on an armed assault on trucks hauling coal during the strike, viewed by prosecutors as an intentional attack on interstate-commerce transportation that carried an obvious risk of lethal harm.

He was convicted in federal court under the statute criminalizing the damaging of motor vehicles used in interstate commerce when done with reckless disregard for human safety. The case has remained a reference point for how the federal system approached strike-linked violence, treating the incident as both sabotage of commerce and a grave act of endangerment.

profiles.name: Arthur Majid Barnes
profiles.description: Arthur Majid Barnes, also reported as Arthur Majeed Barnes, was a member of the Black Men’s Movement Against Crack. New York State Police arrested Barnes, Abdul Haqq Muhammad, and Robert “R.T.” Taylor during a traffic stop in upstate New York on July 16, 1987. Barnes was later imprisoned on weapons-possession convictions and was listed at Sing Sing in 1989 under state prisoner number 88-A-7424.
